newsitem.title: UK: LME copper ends firm, spreads tighten.
newsitem.headline: LME copper ends firm, spreads tighten.

text.p: Copper prices charged higher during late Wednesday LME trading, erasing morning losses and coming within a a whisker of clearing $2,380 per tonne.

Traders said the smart bounce from an early low of $2,325 was a clear example of the market's present volatility and susceptibility to sudden movements in the spread. Backwardations widened out this afternoon, while buy-stops and local speculators kicked in above $2,350.
"It goes to show that this a dangerous old beast at times. Some people may have been tempted to go short at the lows. If so, they got burnt," one said.
Others said the short-term fundamentals of strike action in Chile at Escondida, with another strike vote taking place later on Wednesday at Quebrada Blanca, stemmed further declines.
Meanwhile, the spreads tightened up, with some talk that stocks would be lower again on Thursday after today's increase in inventories which was the first since February.
The cash/threes backwardation, which narrowed to under $60 at one stage on Wednesday, was back around $88 by the close, albeit a long way off Monday's high water-mark of $210.

Three months prices closed at $2,379, up $19 a tonne from the previous day's kerb. Traders see the market remaining prone to wide price fluctuations, with a possible $2,320/2,380 jobbing range developing.
Elsewhere, the rest of the metals complex grabbed copper's coat tails and advanced during the latter part of the day, although only aluminium saw reasonable activity, they said.

Aluminium managed to climb above stubborn resistance around $1,640 during the kerb, and the current steady upside progress is construed technically constructive. There is also the July tightness lingering in the background. Final trade was at $1,645, up $7.50.
Nickel prices extended an earlier uptick during the kerb, with some chart-based buying kicking in due to a confirmed break above $7,300. Last business was at $7,380, up $100.
Lead and zinc both notched up reasonable advances during the kerb also, with the former metal arresting a slide that left it at at 18-month lows on Tuesday.

Business was largely routine, however, with lead ending at $624, up $9. Zinc avoided a test of a downside gap, and broke back above $1,270 instead to conclude the day at $1,273, up $8 from the previous kerb.

Tin conditions remained subdued throughout, and the steadier price indications were a reflection of the firmer trend of the complex as a whole. Three months closed at $5,700 a tonne, up $50 from yesterday.
The alloy market was marked steadily higher, and ended at $1,515, up $10 after scattered trades today.
